summary: Discovery with Monarch Security focused on private VPC deployment options. Customer is evaluating Redwood Private with strict network egress controls, VPC peering limitations, and regional residency constraints. Key concerns: private endpoints (PrivateLink/VPC endpoints), ability to use customer-managed KMS, SOC2/ISO compliance artifacts, and connectivity patterns for on-prem and multi-region apps.
topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway
Customer-managed KMS/HSM and encryption at rest
Networking ports, NAT/firewall rules, and egress control
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lydia Torres (Monarch - Head of Cloud Security), Raj Patel (Monarch - SRE), Kim Alvarez (Monarch - CTO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we really appreciate the time. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Ethan is our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Lydia Torres: Hi, Lydia here. Thanks, Maya. We tried to keep this focused on VPC/private connectivity, network controls, and any compliance touchpoints.
[00:20] Ethan Park: Great. We'll walk through our Private deployment patterns, how endpoints work, and then dig into any specifics — CIDR, peering, and region constraints.
[00:30] Kim Alvarez: Perfect. To frame it: Monarch's putting the inference layer behind our control plane. We need to make sure there are no public egress, and traffic goes over our peering or PrivateLink.
[00:42] Raj Patel: Also important: we run multi-region services and have limited CIDR space, we want to avoid overlapping ranges and prefer transit-gateway style hub-and-spoke if possible.
[00:55] Ethan Park: Understood. High-level: Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC via customer VPC peering or by setting up PrivateLink endpoints, depending on your cloud. For AWS specifically we support VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) to expose the control plane and inference endpoints privately.
[01:12] Lydia Torres: When you say control plane—what stays in Redwood's network vs ours? We need to document what leaves our account.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Good question. There are two flavors. Option A: Private with a control plane managed by Redwood but with private endpoints into your VPC — in that model the inference traffic stays in your VPC for data plane calls. Option B: Fully customer-managed private deployment where the entire control plane runs in your VPC (on-prem or VPC), which we can discuss as an on-prem package. 
[01:36] Lydia Torres: Hmm. For compliance we prefer customer-managed control plane or at minimum private endpoints with no internet egress for inference data.
[01:44] Ethan Park: We can do private endpoints so inference requests resolve to an ENI inside your VPC — traffic never hits the public internet. For model weights and updates there is an initial sync that can be pulled over the private link, or we can do an air-gapped transfer for highly regulated setups.
[02:00] Kim Alvarez: Can you detail the DNS flow? We have strict split-horizon DNS and require that hostnames resolve to private IPs only.
[02:08] Ethan Park: Yes, in AWS we provision an interface endpoint and give you a service name. Your VPC DNS will resolve the redwood api host to the endpoint's private IP. If you have split-horizon, you can override accordingly.
[02:18] Raj Patel: What about cross-region? Our app in us-east-1 needs to reach endpoints in us-west-2 — does traffic cross regions or do we host per-region?
[02:26] Maya Chen: We recommend hosting model replicas in each region for latency-sensitive workloads. Redwood Private supports region-specific deployments; however, some customers opt to peer VPCs across regions or use transit gateway for cross-region routing. There are cost and latency tradeoffs.
[02:40] Lydia Torres: Our blocker is we can't expand CIDR ranges in our main account due to legacy infra. So peering could be tricky because of overlaps.
[02:48] Ethan Park: Right, in that case PrivateLink/Interface endpoints are usually the better path — they don't require non-overlapping CIDRs because they're endpoint-based. Transit Gateway needs non-overlapping.
[02:58] Kim Alvarez: Does PrivateLink support high throughput for large batch inference? We're doing embeddings at scale, and need sustained throughput.
[03:07] Ethan Park: Interface endpoints scale with ENIs and we can provision multiple endpoints or use multiple ENIs. For sustained high throughput we often recommend a mix — dedicated capacity in-region for heavy workloads and PrivateLink for secure connectivity. Some customers use VPC peering for very high throughput if CIDRs allow.
[03:25] Raj Patel: Are there ports we need to open outbound from our app subnets? Our security team hates wide-open egress.
[03:32] Ethan Park: Minimal rules: outbound to the endpoint's IPs on HTTPS 443. If you're doing metrics or trace shipping to Redwood observability we can provide separate endpoints or use existing secure channels. We'll give a port checklist — it's really just HTTPS over the PrivateLink, plus any management ports for agent syncing if you run a customer-managed control plane.
[03:50] Lydia Torres: KMS — we need to use our CMK for encryption at rest. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS?
[03:57] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS with customer CMKs). We can also integrate with HSMs for more advanced key controls.
[04:07] Kim Alvarez: And audit logs? We need to keep model request logs for 365 days and they must be sent to our S3 bucket in a specific region.
[04:15] Ethan Park: We can route logs to your S3 via VPC endpoints (S3 gateway endpoints) or forward logs into your logging pipeline. For retention and residency we can configure log delivery to a specific region and guard it with bucket policies.
[04:28] Raj Patel: How do upgrades/rollouts work? If you push a model version, does it fetch weights over the private link? Any chance of hitting public endpoints during deploy?
[04:36] Ethan Park: Deploys pull model weights over the same private connectivity if configured. We also support a push model where we provide an encrypted bundle that you can stage locally in your VPC. So zero public egress is achievable.
[04:47] Lydia Torres: What about SSO, audit access — we need RBAC via SAML.
[04:53] Maya Chen: We support SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC in our console. For Private deployments the control plane can be plumbed into your IdP via SAML and we push logs to your audit pipeline.
[05:03] Kim Alvarez: Any constraints on region availability for certain model types? We occasionally want to run a newer large model and need GPU types that might not be in all regions.
[05:12] Ethan Park: Yes, model placement depends on underlying GPU availability. Redwood maintains a model catalog with region-performance profiles. For Private deployments, you can pick which region(s) to host models in; if a model requires a particular GPU, we may recommend a nearby region or a dedicated capacity reservation. We'll share our region-model matrix.
[05:26] Raj Patel: If we do a hybrid — Private in VPC for inference and Redwood Hosted for backups/fallback — how do you handle failover while keeping data private?
[05:35] Maya Chen: Typical pattern: we use model variant routing with fallbacks. For sensitive data you can mark routes to disallow fallback to hosted. For non-sensitive, the fallback can route to hosted endpoints. We can enforce policies per route.
[05:49] Lydia Torres: Ok, can you walk us through an example architecture?
[05:52] Ethan Park: Sure. Example A: App in your private subnets -> VPC Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink) -> Redwood Private inference fleet in your VPC (or a managed service that attaches an ENI into your VPC). Control plane traffic also goes via a separate interface endpoint to a control plane service. Logging goes to your logging VPC via peering or to S3 via gateway endpoints.
[06:12] Kim Alvarez: If we wanted to keep weights inside our account, is that supported?
[06:18] Ethan Park: Yes, if you want full control we provide a customer-managed deployment where the model artifacts are stored in your S3 and the runtime runs in your VPC — Redwood provides orchestration and support.
[06:27] Raj Patel: Any firewall/NACL gotchas? We've got very strict NACLs on our subnets.
[06:33] Ethan Park: NACLs are stateless, so ensure ephemeral port ranges allowed if you're using certain protocols. For HTTPS to endpoint ENIs, just allow outbound 443 and established inbound ephemeral. We'll provide exact CIDR/IPs or recommend using security groups for more flexible rules.
[06:48] Lydia Torres: How do you handle TLS and certs for private endpoints?
[06:53] Maya Chen: TLS is terminated at the endpoint and mutual TLS can be configured for additional assurance. Certificates can be managed by Redwood or you can bring your certs depending on the deployment model.
[07:05] Raj Patel: We run RedHat satellite internally and have some legacy VPNs to on-prem. Can we route traffic from on-prem apps to the PrivateLink?
[07:13] Ethan Park: Yes, if your on-prem is connected via VPN or Direct Connect to the VPC with the interface endpoint, traffic flows over that link. For higher throughput we recommend Direct Connect or private interconnects.
[07:24] Kim Alvarez: SLA expectations — if we're running critical inference, what uptime and latency SLOs do you commit to on Private deployments?
[07:31] Maya Chen: For Dedicated and Private we offer SLA-backed uptime depending on the contract. Latency SLOs are defined per workload and instance type. We can share our SLA doc and propose target latency percentiles based on the model and hardware.
[07:44] Lydia Torres: Any compliance artifacts you can share right away? SOC2, ISO, penetration tests?
[07:50] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share the SOC2 report and pen test summary in the security pack. For customer-managed private, some controls shift to you but we provide our controls and integration points.
[07:59] Raj Patel: Who from Redwood manages network setup — do you have a network engineer or is that handed to our cloud infra team?
[08:05] Ethan Park: Typically our SEs (like me) provide a runbook and we can do a joint implementation call with your cloud team. We don't directly modify your VPC — we provide IaC and step-by-step instructions.
[08:16] Maya Chen: Quick qualification questions — what's your timeline and success criteria?
[08:20] Kim Alvarez: Timeline is end of Q2 pilot, production by Q4. Success is: <=50ms p99 latency for small gen requests, embedding throughput of X tokens/sec, and SOC2 audit readiness.
[08:33] Lydia Torres: Also must be fully private for customer PII paths and logs stored in our region for at least 365 days.
[08:40] Maya Chen: Noted. We can scope a pilot — suggested steps: 1) deep-dive network runbook, 2) pilot in one region with PrivateLink and a small Dedicated pool, 3) measure latency/throughput and iterate.
[08:54] Raj Patel: Cost — what's the expected delta vs hosted? We're happy to pay for Private but need an estimate.
[09:00] Maya Chen: We'll send a preliminary cost estimate: Dedicated node pricing + network egress (minimal if private) and any implementation fees. We'll include options for reserved capacity to lower unit cost.
[09:10] Kim Alvarez: One more: do you support using our internal CA for mutual TLS?
[09:15] Ethan Park: Yes, mTLS with customer-supplied certs is supported in Private deployments. We'll include cert rotation guidance.
[09:23] Lydia Torres: Are there vendor lock-in risks if we go with Redwood Private? For instance, how easy is it to migrate models and infra out later?
[09:31] Maya Chen: We try to minimize lock-in — artifacts are standard (model files in S3 or OCI), and we can provide export tooling. Operationally, if you run customer-managed, it's your infra so migration is straightforward.
[09:43] Raj Patel: For the pilot, what do you need from us network-wise?
[09:47] Ethan Park: CIDR blocks for VPCs, boolean about overlapping ranges, expected throughput numbers, your preferred region for the pilot, and contact for your cloud infra team. We'll provide Terraform snippets for creating interface endpoints and security group rules.
[10:00] Kim Alvarez: Let's talk about the scenario where CIDR overlaps prevent peering and PrivateLink is used. Any limitations with security groups and ENI scaling?
[10:08] Ethan Park: Security groups are fine; you can attach them to endpoints. ENI scaling is generally transparent — if you need heavy concurrency we provision multiple endpoints and load-balance across them. There's a small management overhead but it's supported.
[10:24] Lydia Torres: Data residency: logs and telemetry must stay in our region, can you ensure that?
[10:30] Ethan Park: Yes — logs can be routed to your S3 in-region; for telemetry we can configure collectors to only forward to your endpoints. We'll mark the route as region-locked in the pilot config.
[10:42] Maya Chen: Any other blockers on your side?
[10:44] Raj Patel: Licensing procurement will want a simple contract with SLAs and indemnities. Also need to run an internal network test.
[10:52] Maya Chen: We'll coordinate legal and procurement artifacts.
[10:55] Kim Alvarez: Can you share a sample terraform snippet now?
[10:58] Ethan Park: I'll include the snippet in the follow-up — it's a small module to create interface endpoints, route53 private DNS entries, and the security group rules.
[11:08] Lydia Torres: One clarification: for model updates do you support patch windows and maintenance windows to avoid unexpected pulls during business hours?
[11:15] Ethan Park: Yes, maintenance windows can be scheduled and model syncs can be throttled; we'll ensure no disruptive pulls during your windows.
[11:24] Raj Patel: If we do cross-account deployment (shared services VPC hosting the inference), is that supported?
[11:31] Ethan Park: Yes — we support cross-account endpoints and we can set up IAM roles for cross-account access. For PrivateLink across accounts, you share the service and accept it in the consumer account.
[11:44] Maya Chen: Ok, to recap the next steps: we'll send the architecture doc + terraform, security pack, region-model matrix, cost estimate, and propose a technical deep-dive next Tuesday.
[11:58] Kim Alvarez: Sounds good. We'll send our CIDRs and a point person for the cloud infra team.
[12:04] Lydia Torres: And we'll want the SOC2 and pen test artifacts before the procurement review.
[12:11] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll get those by EOD tomorrow.
[12:16] Raj Patel: Thanks all.
[12:18] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and scheduling.

Notes: Transcript contains occasional miscues and short overlaps. Some product names may be transcribed imperfectly (e.g., PrivateLink vs Privatelink).
